entries.meaning: The forest people continued: “Blessed are the land, woods, paths, and hills wherever you have set your feet, Lord. Blessed are the birds and forest-roaming animals; their births have borne fruit through seeing you. We and our families are blessed, for our eyes have filled themselves with your vision. You have thoughtfully chosen a good dwelling, pleasant in every season. We shall serve in every way, warding off elephants, lions, snakes, and tigers. The tangled woods, mountains, caverns, and caves are all familiar to us step by step. Wherever you go we shall arrange your hunts and show you lakes, waterfalls, and watering places. We are your servants with all our households; do not hesitate, Lord, to command us.” The Lord, compassion’s very abode and beyond Vedic speech and sages’ minds, listened to the Kirātas’ words as a father listens to a child’s speech.

Rāma cherishes love alone—let whoever would understand, understand this. He then satisfied all the forest dwellers, nurturing their love with gentle speech. They bowed their heads and departed, returning home while telling and hearing the Lord’s virtues. In this way the two brothers lived in the forest with Sītā, bringing joy to gods and sages. From the moment Raghunāyaka settled there, the forest became a source of blessing. Trees of many kinds flowered and fruited; beautiful, curving, excellent vines made canopies. Naturally lovely like wish-fulfilling trees, they seemed to have left the gods’ forest and come there. Rows of bees hummed more sweetly, and a threefold breeze blew, bringing delight. Blue-throated birds, melodious cuckoos, parrots, cātakas, cakravākas, and cakoras called in varied ways, pleasing the ear and stealing the heart.

Elephants, lions, monkeys, and wild forest animals wandered together with enmity gone. Hunting animals became especially delighted as they roamed and saw Rāma’s beauty. The gods praised Rāma’s forest after seeing every divine grove that exists in the world. The Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Yamunā, blessed Narmadā, and Godāvarī, and all lakes, seas, rivers, and streams extolled Mandākinī. The mountains of sunrise and sunset, Kailāsa, Mandara, Meru, every divine abode, and all mountains beginning with Himālaya sang Citrakūṭa’s fame. Vindhya’s glad heart could not contain its joy, for it had gained immense renown without toil. Gods declared day and night that Citrakūṭa’s birds, animals, vines, trees, and every kind of grass were blessed stores of merit.

Those possessing eyes beheld Raghubara, gained the fruit of birth, and became free of grief. Even immobile creatures, touched by the dust of his feet, rejoiced and became entitled to the highest state. That naturally beautiful forest and mountain was filled with blessing and supremely purifying; how can one relate the greatness of the place where the ocean of happiness made his home? Rāma had left the ocean of milk and abandoned Ayodhyā to dwell there with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. Even a hundred thousand thousand-mouthed Śeṣas could not describe the forest’s loveliness; how then can I tell it—a pond turtle attempting to lift Mount Mandara? Lakṣmaṇa served in deed, thought, and word; his character and love cannot be recounted. Moment by moment he watched the feet of Sītā and Rāma and recognized their affection toward him; not even in a dream did he turn his mind to brother, mother, father, or home.

Living with Rāma, Sītā was happy and forgot the city, relatives, and home. Moment by moment she gazed upon her beloved’s moonlike face and rejoiced like a young cakora. Seeing her husband’s love increase each day, she remained delighted like a cakravāka in daylight. Her mind was devoted to Rāma’s feet, and the forest seemed dearer than a thousand Ayodhyās. The leaf hut was dear because her beloved was beside her; deer and birds were her cherished family, and sages and sages’ wives were like parents-in-law. Tubers, roots, and fruit were like nectar; a grass pallet was delightful with her Lord beside her, as comforting as Love’s own couch. Could worldly luxury overpower her, when the guardians of the worlds themselves arise through beholding her? People remembering Rāma discard sensual luxury like straw; nothing of this is surprising in Sītā, Rāma’s beloved and the world’s mother.

Raghunātha did and said whatever would bring Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa happiness. He recounted ancient tales, and Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā listened with deep delight. Whenever Rāma remembered Ayodhyā, however, his eyes filled with water. Recalling mothers, father, relatives, brothers, and Bharata’s affection, character, and service, the compassionate Lord became sorrowful. Reflecting on the harshness of the time, he regained composure; seeing him so affected, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa became distressed, like a shadow following a person. Perceiving his beloved and brother’s condition, the steadfast and gracious Raghunandana, sandalwood to devotees’ hearts, began telling sacred stories; hearing them, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā found comfort. Rāma shone with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā in the leaf dwelling as Indra dwells in Amarāvatī with Śacī and Jayanta.

The Lord cared for Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa as eyelids guard the pupils of the eyes. Lakṣmaṇa served Sītā and Raghubīra with the undivided absorption with which an undiscerning person serves the body. Thus the Lord lived happily in the forest, bringing welfare to birds, animals, gods, and ascetics. Having told of Rāma’s lovely journey into the forest, the poet turns to how Sumantra returned to Ayodhyā. Guha came back after escorting the Lord and saw the chariot with the minister. When the Niṣāda saw the minister distraught, his own grief became indescribable. Crying “Rāma! Rāma! Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa!” Sumantra fell heavily upon the ground. Looking southward, the horses neighed like wingless birds in anguish. They neither grazed grass nor drank water but shed tears; all the Niṣādas were distressed to see Raghubara’s horses.

Mastering himself, Guha said, “Sumantra, now put grief aside. You are learned and know the highest truth; take courage upon seeing that Fate has turned away.” Recounting various stories in gentle language, he brought Sumantra by force to sit in the chariot. Slackened by sorrow, the minister could not drive: the pain of separation from Raghubara remained lodged in his heart. The horses thrashed about and would not move along the road, as though wild deer had been harnessed to the chariot. They stumbled, fell, and looked back, frantic in separation and pierced by grief. Whoever uttered “Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Vaidehī,” they neighed repeatedly and looked toward that well-wisher. How can the horses’ state in separation be told? They were as distressed as serpents deprived of their jewels. Seeing minister and horses overcome by grief, Guha called four good servants and sent them with the charioteer.

Guha escorted the charioteer and returned; the anguish of separation cannot be described. The Niṣādas took the chariot toward Ayodhyā, repeatedly sinking into grief along the road. Sumantra brooded, broken and wretched: “Shame on a life without Raghubīra! This base body did not perish at the last, nor earn honor by dying when parted from him. My life has become a vessel of infamy and sin—why does it not depart? Alas, dull mind, you missed the moment; even now the heart does not split in two.” He wrung his hands, beat his head, and lamented like a miser who has lost a hoard of wealth. It was as though a celebrated champion, bound by his reputation as a noble warrior, had fled the battle. His remorse resembled that of a noble, discerning, Veda-knowing brahmin of approved conduct who had unknowingly drunk intoxicating liquor.

Sumantra’s heart burned terribly, like that of a wise, virtuous, high-born wife, devoted to her husband in deed, thought, and word, who through the force of circumstances must leave him. His eyes were wet and his vision dim; his bewildered mind could scarcely hear. His lips dried and his mouth seemed sealed, yet life would not leave because the heart’s doors barred it. He became so discolored he could not be looked at, as though he had killed his father and mother. A vast sense of loss and shame possessed his mind, like a sinner dreading the road to Yama’s city. Words would not come; inwardly he lamented: “Why should I go and see Ayodhyā? Whoever sees the chariot without Rāma will shrink from looking at me. When the city’s anguished men and women run to question me, what answer shall I give them after planting a thunderbolt in every heart?”
